title: Having the Feedback Conversation
author: Peter Foster
summary: Pete Foster closes a three-part series on giving teachers feedback with a granular breakdown of the conversation itself, structured around a 'Praise, Problem, Action' arc. In the Praise stage, he asks a prepared question designed to help teachers form and check their own mental model of effective practice, pushing back if the teacher deflects to the negative. In the Problem stage, he uses diagnostic questions to gauge how well a teacher already understands a weaker area before selectively sharing evidence, calibrating probing versus direct evidence-sharing based on the teacher's own responses. In the Action stage, he asks the teacher for their own solution first before offering his own, to build motivation and ownership, and closes with concrete mechanisms -- modelling with non-examples, planning implementation into upcoming lessons, or physical nudges -- to ensure the conversation produces real classroom change.
points: Foster structures every feedback conversation around a three-part arc: Praise (form and check mental models of effective practice), Problem (establish reality and a route forward via diagnostic questions and evidence), and Action (define success criteria and engineer next steps).
He deliberately adapts each conversation to two variables: the specific teacher's experience and personality, and how the teacher actually answers the questions asked, not a fixed script.

In the Problem stage, he calibrates directness based on the diagnostic question's answer, moving straight to shared evidence if the teacher shows clear understanding, but probing further if the teacher reveals a misconception.

In the Action stage, he asks teachers for their own proposed fix before offering his own, arguing this builds 'motivational and implementation benefits' by working with what the teacher already partially does.
quotes: There will always be Praise, Problem and Action but how these things go will vary quite significantly from teacher to teacher and lesson to lesson.

It adapts to the teacher. If I know the teacher well and have worked with them before, we'll obviously discuss previous feedback and actions but we'll also have shared understanding of some of the problems their facing.
If the teacher reveals an incomplete understanding of the focus area (or a misconception), probe further to make sure you’re clear.

It's worth asking this question even if we have a clear idea of an action that tackles the problem we've defined... the teacher may have a strategy close to what they already do that addresses the problem.

Perhaps controversially, I don't think every solution to every classroom problem can be practiced... Not every improvement a teacher makes will be a practicable behaviour. Some will be shifts in planning, understanding or knowledge.
